title: Why He Took His Car Battery to Bed

lot.desc: a logging camp in snowy pines: a gravel truck lot under a yard light, a row of crew pickups with HALVORSEN TIMBER doors, the foreman's giant red truck, the hero's small old car, a snowplow, the plank bunkhouse with a porch, a thermometer on the post, the mess hall with a clock, log piles, fuel drums, a sawhorse
lot.light: night: blue moonlight + one warm yard light + warm windows; day: crisp low winter sun; dawn at forty below: low pink-orange sun through ice fog
lot.time: night 5-12 s and 28-30 s; day 23-28 s and 58-61 s; dawn 2.5-5 s and 30-58 s

bunk.desc: a plank bunkhouse: double bunks with wool blankets, a glowing wood stove with a kettle, long johns and socks drying on a line, boots, a card table with a lantern, a frosted window, axes and a calendar on the wall
bunk.light: warm firelight from the stove + one hanging bulb, cool blue from the window

mess.desc: the mess hall: long plank tables, benches, plates of pancakes, coffee urn, the cook's counter and an old fridge, a chalk menu board, antlers, windows onto snow
mess.light: cool morning window light + warm pendant lamps

hero.look: orange quilted puffy parka with a zipper, chest pocket and a reflective patch; blue knit beanie with a pompom; brass key on a red string

foreman.look: green-and-black buffalo plaid mackinaw, red trapper hat with ear flaps, big grey moustache, suspenders, a steaming mug

crew.look: canvas and wool work jackets, beanies, beards

cook.look: white apron with a red trim over a striped shirt, paper cap, bald with a beard

lines.text: He tucked his car battery into bed every night,
and his was the only engine in camp that started.
Every night at the logging camp, the new guy lugs all forty pounds of it inside.
The foreman laughs, "Gonna read it a bedtime story too?"
lines.speaker: foreman

lines.text: Night one, it sleeps by the stove.
Night two, it gets a blanket.
Night three, it gets his pillow, and he sleeps on the floor.
By breakfast, the whole camp calls him the battery babysitter.
Why? He won't say.
The first cold morning, every truck starts just fine, and the foreman honks at him all the way to work.
Then one night, it hits forty below.
At six, the whole crew turns their keys, and the lot goes click, click, click.
Even the foreman's giant truck just coughs and dies.
Then the babysitter walks out with his battery steaming in his arms, hooks it up, and turns the key.
First try.
You see, a battery makes power with a chemical reaction,
and the cold slows it down like honey from the fridge.
At forty below, it loses more than half its power,
just when a frozen engine needs twice as much.
So the foreman shuffles over, "Hey, babysitter, got cables?"
lines.speaker: foreman

lines.text: By lunch, the babysitter has jump-started the whole camp.
And that night, the foreman tucks his own battery into bed.
